rows.answer: To recover your partially upgraded application and ensure its data integrity, I've outlined a step-by-step plan for you: 1. **Rollback Database Migrations**: - First, identify which SQL migration scripts were executed during the upgrade. You can find this by looking at the most recent database migrations in your version control system. 2. **Prepare Backup**: - Take a snapshot of your current production state before rolling back to minimize risks. This should include: - A full backup of the entire database, including all tables and data. - A backup of any custom application code deployed on top of the database (e.g., custom plugins, views, stored procedures). 3. **Rollback Database**: - Execute the SQL migration scripts in reverse order to revert your database schema back to a stable point before the upgrade. 4. **Verify Data Integrity**: - Run data integrity checks against the restored backup. This will help identify any missing or corrupted data that may have been introduced during the roll back process. - Compare data between the rollback state and the original production state to ensure no data loss occurred during the rollback. 5. **Re-test Application**: - Verify the application functions correctly after the database has been rolled back. This should include testing all user flows, error handling, authentication, and any other critical application functionality. - If any issues are found, identify their root cause and prioritize them based on business impact before moving forward with the rollback. 6. **Revert to Production**: - Once you're confident that your data integrity is restored and the application functions correctly after the database has been rolled back, you can restore your production environment to its original state. Remember to document all steps, including any issues encountered or potential risks identified during the process. This will help in case of a future incident where you need to re-run this rollback procedure.

Rollback Database Migrations: - First, identify which SQL migration scripts were executed during the upgrade. You can find this by looking at the migration log files or the database schema changes tracked by the version control system. 2. Revert to Last Known Good State: - Next, switch your development database back to the last known stable state before the upgrade began. This may be a snapshot from a backup taken just before you started the upgrade process. - If available, revert the schema to the point of the most recent backup that was validated as good. 3. Verify Schema Integrity: - Run the following SQL queries on your database after rolling back to ensure data integrity: ```sql SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'your_database_name' AND table_type = 'BASE TABLE'; SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.views; SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'your_database_name'; SHOW tables; SHOW views; ``` - These queries should help identify any missing or orphaned database objects after the rollback. 4. Re-run Upgrade Tests: - Finally, re-run the upgrade tests you initially ran before starting the migration process to ensure that everything works as expected now that your application has been rolled back to a stable state. - You can run these tests in parallel with rolling out your initial migration sequence so that if any issues are found during testing, you have time to address them. 5. Perform Post-mortem Analysis: - After rollback and before proceeding with the upgrade, it is important to thoroughly review what went wrong and why the database upgrade failed. - Identify the root cause of the failure so that it doesn't happen again in future upgrades. 6. Backup the Database Before Proceeding: - Always create a backup of your production database before proceeding with any changes or migrations so that you can roll back if something goes wrong. Remember, the key to avoiding data loss during an application upgrade is proper planning and testing beforehand, as well as having a good backup strategy in place.

rows.question: A team must move a legacy app into production deployment within 4 weeks. There are no tests, poor docs, and a shaky backup story. Produce a realistic migration plan with sequencing, risk controls, and rollback.
rows.answer: To smoothly migrate your fragile legacy application into disciplined production deployment within four weeks, I've outlined a detailed step-by-step staged deployment plan for you: 1. **Preparation**: - Gather any available documentation about the system architecture, dependencies, configuration settings, and migration procedures. - Review and consolidate existing test cases that were previously run against this application to identify their current state of completeness and quality. - Verify the integrity of your backup strategy and ensure you have access to a working backup from at least one point in time before migration. 2. **Testing & Validation**: - Develop new automated tests to validate the migration procedure, including regression tests for existing functionality that may be impacted by the migration process. - Run these tests against both the source codebase and the target environment to ensure they work as expected. 3. **Infrastructure Preparation**: - Set up a staging environment that mirrors your production environment as closely as possible in terms of infrastructure configuration, database schema, and runtime environment settings. - Deploy the application and its dependencies into this staging environment, ensuring that it is configured identically to the target production environment. 4. **Migration Execution**: - Plan the migration procedure, including any necessary data transformations or manipulations. - Carefully execute the migration in small increments, applying just one change at a time. - Monitor for errors and rollback immediately if you encounter any issues that could cause system instability or loss of data. 5. **Post-migration Validation**: - Run your automated tests against both the staging and production environments to confirm that they pass without issue. - Monitor system performance and stability in production over a period of time to ensure it meets expected levels. 6. **Rollback Procedure**: - Develop a clear rollback procedure, including scripts or documentation for each step needed to revert back to the source codebase if necessary. - Test your rollback procedure in a staging environment before proceeding to production deployment. 7. **Documentation & Training**: - Document your migration process and ensure that it is available to any team members who may need to understand the steps involved or troubleshoot issues related to the migration. - Develop training materials to help educate new employees about your application, its architecture, and the importance of maintaining a stable production environment. By following this staged plan, you should be able to successfully migrate your legacy app into production in just four weeks.
